definition: Amorphous means without definite shape or type.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word amorphous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know amorphous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By August the community garden had grown amorphous, its plots dissolving into one another with no path or fence to say where anything began.
A loose arrangement still has a shape with slack in it; amorphous goes further - no shape ever existed to loosen.
A fluid lineup changes shape from week to week, but at any given moment it has one; amorphous means there is never a shape to point to at all.

Shapeless is the plain, everyday word for having no outline at all - a shapeless bag, a shapeless afternoon. Amorphous does the same job in formal dress and reaches further, to structure and type: an amorphous committee lacks not just edges but any organizing plan to sort it by.

Formless is the loftier, more poetic cousin - mist, chaos, the void before creation. Amorphous keeps its feet on the ground: clay, crowds, committees. Reach for formless when you want grandeur, and for amorphous when you are describing something structureless in a plain, exact, almost scientific way.

The ceramics teacher thumped a fresh bag of clay onto each wheel.
'It arrives amorphous,' she said, poking the gray lump, 'no edges, no front, no plan - and it will happily stay that way forever.
Your job this term is to talk it into a shape.'
Amorphous is the right word because the clay lacks definite shape of any kind - not a broken shape, not a changing shape, no shape.
Disorganized things have parts in the wrong places; the lump has no places.
That 'without form at all' meaning is the word's whole job.
neutral / slightly technical
Amorphous is for things and organizations that lack shape or structure - a crowd, a blob, a committee without borders.
Its cluster-mate nebulous is for ideas and plans that stay cloudy.
A jellyfish is amorphous; a jellyfish-shaped career plan is nebulous.
If parts exist but sit in the wrong places, say disorganized instead.

Mapmakers hate towns like Alder Creek.
Ask where it ends and you get a shrug: the streets thin out, the lots widen, and somewhere past the feed store the town simply stops being the town.
The county's own atlas calls the settlement amorphous, and the word is doing precise work.
There is no boundary line to draw, and never was one.
It is not that the border moved, or that it is disputed.
Rival towns fight over lines that exist; Alder Creek never had a line to fight over.
Incorporation would fix that, the county clerk points out.
A vote, a charter, a filed map — and edges would exist for the first time.
Until then, the atlas leaves a dotted smudge where a boundary should be, the cartographer's honest confession that there is no shape to record.
